blocks.text: Introduction
Hi, and welcome to Small Models, Real Systems, the weekly research digest by Mylari. This is edition four, for Wednesday the twenty-first of October, 2026.
This week: five picks where each part of the job goes to the cheapest thing that does it well. And a sharp reminder of what happens when the labels change.
Amazon - copy the span, generate only the rest

First, Amazon, in a paper posted on the fifteenth. Product attribute extraction usually means a generative model writes every value out, token by token. But about four in five values in their catalog data appear word for word in the listing.

So they added a tagging head to a fine-tuned Qwen3 model of just zero point six billion parameters. It checks the five hundred most common attributes in one pass and copies the matching span from the text.

The generator only writes the rest: rare attributes, and inferred values like cuisine or diet type. Recall rose from about seventy to eighty percent, precision held at ninety-seven, and response time fell by forty-four percent.
LY Corporation - encoders pre-trained on your own text

Second, LY Corporation, the company behind LINE and Yahoo Japan, in an engineering post from the fifteenth. Their Moegi project pre-trains BERT-style encoders on each service's own text and shares them across teams.

On three classification tasks from Yahoo Shopping and Yahoo Search, the hundred-and-ten-million-parameter model beat two public Japanese encoders of similar size on every task, by up to fourteen points. Against GPT-5.6 Sol with no examples, it won two of three tasks and came close on the third, at nine hundred to seventeen hundred times lower estimated inference cost.
The lesson: put your domain's vocabulary into pre-training once, and share it.
GitHub - regex for recall, an encoder for judgment

Third, GitHub, in a post from the thirteenth, a day before our window. Secret scanning had used a large language model to decide whether a password-shaped string is a real credential. Now regular expressions cast a wide net for candidates, and a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder reads each one with its file path, secret type and nearby code.

Training leaned on hard negatives like test fixtures, checksums and documentation examples, and near-duplicates were kept out of the test set. Against the old pipeline: thirteen percent higher precision, nineteen percent higher recall, scans eighty-six percent faster, and serving cost down more than ninety-eight percent. In a live test, owner-weighted alert acceptance rose eleven and a half percent.
Shravan Pendem - seven queues the model had never seen

Fourth, a careful trial by engineer Shravan Pendem, published on the seventeenth. He fine-tuned Qwen 3.5 at zero point eight billion parameters to route bank messages into seventy queues, using the public Banking seventy-seven dataset.

With thirty-two labels per queue it scored eighty-seven percent, ahead of Claude Sonnet given only queue names, at eighty-one and a half. But with one written line describing each queue, Sonnet reached eighty-eight.
Only the model trained on every label stayed clearly ahead, at ninety-three. Then the bank added seven queues. Claude handled them by editing its list.
The trained model misrouted all but six of two hundred and eighty new-queue messages. His advice: describe your queues first, and name who retrains before launch.
BanglaShield - a compact safety classifier across scripts

Fifth, safety classification in Bangla, from Manchester, Notre Dame, Lancaster and the Islamic University of Technology, posted on the sixteenth. Bangla is written in native script, in Latin letters, and code-mixed with English, Hindi or Urdu. Six large language models labelled forty-seven percent of unsafe native-script prompts as safe, and sixty-three percent once romanized.

A fine-tuned MuRIL encoder of about two hundred and thirty-seven million parameters reached eighty-four to eighty-eight macro F1 on every form, more than forty points ahead of the best large model. The catch: trained on native script alone, it scored under forty on romanized prompts. It needed romanized prompts in its training mix.
Patterns this week and sign-off
The pattern this week: give each part of the job to the cheapest thing that does it well. Copy spans instead of generating them, filter with rules before a classifier, and pre-train on your own text.
But plan for change. New queues and new scripts broke models that looked great on their test sets. Links and numbers are in the show notes.
Thanks for listening, and see you next Wednesday.
